note.overview: Battery swapping for electric vehicle refueling is reviving and thriving. Despite a captivating sustainable future where swapping batteries will be as convenient as refueling gas today, a tension is mounting in practice (beyond the traditional “range anxiety” issue): On one hand, it is desirable to maximize battery proximity and availability to customers. On the other hand, capacitated urban power grids may curb decentralized charging at a slow speed.

source.quote: To reconcile this tension, some cities are embracing an emerging infrastructure network: Decentralized swapping stations replenish charged batteries from centralized charging stations.

Given the set of swapping stations I (which achieves a prespecified level of proximity to cus­ tomers) and the set of feasible charging locations H, the decision variables include whether to select location h ∈ H to build a charging station, denoted by zh = 1 or 0, whether to allocate the swapping station i ∈I to be served by a charging station h, denoted by yih = 1 or 0, and the battery reorder quantity from the charging sta­ tion h to the swapping station i, denoted by Qih ≥0.
Each swapping station adopts an (r, Q) policy to replenish its inventory of charged batteries.
Together, the pre­ vious setup forms the basis for modeling the operations and design of citywide battery swapping service net­ works, which the following two sections elaborate on.

That is, once the stock level drops to a reorder level ri, the swap­ ping station operator at location i (with ri + Qi charged batteries at time 0 in stock) will dispatch a truck to send the Qi depleted batteries to the central charging station.
